C005.subject: remote work with high autonomy
C005.object: individual task completion speed more than remote work with low autonomy
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work with high autonomy individual task completion speed more than remote work with low autonomy]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled field experiment comparing task completion times for solo, focused tasks between teams with high vs. low autonomy in remote settings (2020-2023) — Directly tests the causal claim by manipulating autonomy levels and measuring individual task speed in the specified domain and temporal window.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of remote work productivity studies (2020-2023) that stratify by autonomy level and task type — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether high autonomy consistently outperforms low autonomy for solo, focused tasks, addressing the disputed status.

C006.subject: remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work individual task completion speed]

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of controlled experiments comparing task completion times for solo, focused tasks in remote vs. on-site settings (e.g., from journals like Journal of Applied Psychology or Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction) — Synthesizes existing empirical evidence across multiple studies to determine the overall effect size and direction, directly addressing the disputed hypothesis with higher statistical power.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field study using productivity tracking software (e.g., RescueTime or similar) on a cohort of knowledge workers performing standardized solo tasks during standard business hours, with pre-pandemic baseline data for comparison — Provides real-world, time-stamped data on individual task completion speed in remote settings versus controlled on-site baselines, capturing temporal and geographic scope specified in the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model of attention and interruption costs in remote work environments (e.g., based on the attention-restoration theory or the theory of distributed cognition) — Offers a causal framework to explain why remote work might decrease or increase solo task speed, guiding the design of empirical tests and interpreting conflicting results.

qualifier.temporal: during standard business hours, pre-pandemic baseline studies
qualifier.geographic: global, with emphasis on developed countries

C007.subject: remote work with high task interdependence
C007.object: team coordination efficiency more than remote work with low task interdependence
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work with high task interdependence team coordination efficiency more than remote work with low task interdependence]

[PATH:empirical] A meta-analysis of field experiments comparing coordination outcomes (e.g., project completion time, communication frequency) in remote vs. co-located teams with high vs. low task interdependence, controlling for industry and project complexity. — Directly tests the hypothesis by isolating the moderating effect of task interdependence on coordination efficiency in remote settings, using causal evidence from randomized or quasi-experimental designs.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal survey data from knowledge-intensive firms during 2020-2022, measuring perceived coordination efficiency, task interdependence (via validated scales like the Team Interdependence Scale), and remote work intensity. — Provides correlational and temporal evidence within the specified temporal and geographic scope, allowing analysis of how changes in remote work interact with interdependence to affect coordination over the pandemic period.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational simulation modeling of team coordination dynamics (e.g., agent-based models) that varies task interdependence and communication delay (proxy for remote work), to derive theoretical predictions under controlled parameters. — Supports causal inference by isolating mechanisms (e.g., information loss, feedback delays) that may amplify coordination inefficiency under high interdependence, generating testable predictions for empirical validation.

C008.subject: remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work team coordination efficiency]

[PATH:empirical] Meta-analysis of field experiments on remote vs. co-located team coordination in high-collaboration, synchronous software development projects (e.g., from journals like Organization Science or Management Science) — Directly tests the hypothesis by aggregating causal evidence from randomized or quasi-experimental designs, controlling for confounds like tool adoption and task interdependence, which matches the scope and qualifier of the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal archival study using digital trace data (e.g., Slack, Jira, or Git commit logs) from post-2020 organizations in developed economies to measure communication latency, task handoff efficiency, and project completion times — Provides high-resolution, objective behavioral data on coordination efficiency in the specified temporal and geographic context, enabling quantitative confirmation or refutation of the claimed enhancement.

[PATH:theoretical] Review of coordination theory literature (e.g., Malone & Crowston, 1994; Espinosa et al., 2007) applied to remote work with modern digital tools — Helps identify boundary conditions under which remote work might enhance or impair coordination (e.g., reliance on synchronous vs. asynchronous communication), clarifying whether the hypothesis aligns with established mechanisms or requires revision.

qualifier.temporal: post-2020, during widespread adoption of digital collaboration tools
qualifier.geographic: global, with emphasis on organizations in developed economies with high-speed internet infrastructure
